title: 〜てしまう — "ended up", "all of it"
explanation: Add しまう to the て-form to say an action is completely finished, or that something happened that you didn't want: さいふをわすれてしまった, "I (went and) forgot my wallet". It often carries a feeling of "oops" or regret, which makes it perfect for apologies. In casual speech てしまう shrinks to ちゃう (たべちゃった), and でしまう becomes じゃう (のんじゃった); in polite speech say てしまいました. Don't mix it up with ておく, which is for doing something on purpose, ahead of time.

title: 〜たら — "if", "when"
explanation: Take the plain past form and add ら to say "if" or "once (this happens)": いえについたら、でんわして, "call me when you get home"; あめだったら, "if it's raining"; さむかったら, "if you're cold". The たら part always happens first, and the second part can be anything, including a request, a wish or "let's"; 〜たらどう？ means "why don't you …?". It is the most general "if" and works in casual and polite speech alike, since the end of the sentence sets the politeness. とき just means "at the time when", ても means "even if", and ば, と and なら are narrower kinds of "if" that come later.

title: くれる — someone gives to me
explanation: くれる also means "give", but only when the gift comes toward you or someone on your side, like your partner or family: つまがネクタイをくれた, "my wife gave me a tie". The giver takes が (or は) and the receiver, if you say it, takes に (わたしに). Think of the direction: あげる goes out from you, くれる comes in toward you, and もらう tells the same story from the receiver's side (つまにネクタイをもらった). Use くれます in polite speech and くれる with your partner; doing favours (〜てくれる) is the next step.

title: 〜すぎる — "too much"
explanation: Add すぎる to say something is "too …" or that you did something "too much". With verbs, use the ます-stem, the part before ます: たべすぎた, "I ate too much". With い-adjectives drop the final い (たかい → たかすぎる), with な-adjectives just add すぎる (しずかすぎる), and いい becomes よすぎる. すぎる itself works like a る-verb: すぎます and すぎました in polite speech, すぎる, すぎた and すぎない in casual talk, and すぎて to link a reason (からすぎて、たべられない, "it's too spicy to eat"). It usually sounds like a complaint, so you'll hear it after big dinners and in shops.

title: 〜そう — "looks …"
explanation: Add そう to say how something looks to you, before you know for sure: おいしそう, "that looks delicious". い-adjectives drop the い (おいしい → おいしそう), な-adjectives just add そう (げんきそう), and verbs use the ます-stem (ふりそう, "it looks like it'll rain"); two special ones are いい → よさそう and ない → なさそう. Before a noun it becomes そうな (おいしそうなケーキ), before a verb そうに, and you add だ or です at the end for casual or polite speech. Careful: かわいそう means "poor thing", not "looks cute". This そう is only about appearance; そうだ meaning "I heard" and ようだ meaning "it seems" are separate lessons.

pattern: 〜てくれる・〜てもらう・〜てあげる
explanation: Put くれる, もらう or あげる after the て-form to show who is doing a favour for whom. 〜てくれる means someone does something for me (つまがりょうりをつくってくれた), 〜てもらう means I get someone to do it, with that person + に (おっとにてつだってもらった), and 〜てあげる means I do it for someone, which can sound a little showy, so use it with care. To ask your partner for something, say 〜てくれる？, or more politely 〜てもらえますか, and to thank them, say 〜てくれてありがとう. title: 〜ば — "if"
explanation: ば is another "if", built by changing the verb's last u-sound to e and adding ば (いく → いけば, たべる → たべれば, する → すれば, くる → くれば); い-adjectives change い to ければ (やすければ, and いい → よければ), ない becomes なければ, and nouns use なら instead. Two set phrases are worth learning whole: 〜ばいい, "you just need to …", and どうすればいい？, "what should I do?"; 〜ばよかった means "I wish I had …". ば puts the focus on the condition itself, while たら is the all-purpose "if / when" and と is for things that always happen. It is fine in both casual and polite speech; the end of the sentence sets the politeness.

title: 〜し — "and besides"
explanation: Put し after a plain-form sentence to stack up reasons, like "… and besides …": やすいし、おいしいし、ここにしよう, "it's cheap, it's tasty — let's go with this place". Nouns and な-adjectives take だ before し (あめだし, ひまだし). Often people give just one reason with し and leave the rest unsaid, which sounds softer than から: あしたはやすみだし…, "well, tomorrow's a day off, so …". から gives one clear reason, while し hints that there are others too. In polite speech you can put です or ます before し (やすいですし).

title: 〜そうだ — "I heard that"
explanation: Put そうだ (casual) or そうです (polite) after a full plain-form sentence to pass on something you heard or read: あしたはあめだそうです, "I hear it's going to rain tomorrow", and say where it came from with 〜によると, "according to …". Watch the form in front: the plain form (ふるそうだ) means "I heard", but the ます-stem (ふりそうだ) means "it looks like", which is a different lesson. Between partners people often just use って instead (あしたあめだって), and らしい also means "apparently". ようだ is your own guess from evidence, whereas そうだ simply reports what someone said.

title: 〜ておく — "do in advance"
explanation: おく means "put" or "leave", and after the て-form it says you do something now so that it's ready for later: ホテルをよやくしておく, "I'll book the hotel ahead of time". title: 〜と — "whenever", "if (naturally)"
explanation: Put と after the dictionary form (or the ない-form) to say that one thing always or automatically leads to another: ボタンをおすと、ドアがあく, "when you press the button, the door opens". It is perfect for giving directions (みぎにまがると、えきがあります), explaining how machines work, and talking about habits and natural facts. The second half must be something that simply happens, so no requests, wishes or "let's"; for those use たら (いえについたら、でんわして). This と comes after a verb or adjective (a noun needs だ first: あめだと), so it isn't the と that means "and" or "with"; ば and なら are the other "if" words. The end of the sentence sets the politeness, so it works in both casual and polite speech.

title: 〜ようになる — "come to be able"
explanation: Add ようになる to the dictionary form or the potential form to describe a gradual change in what you can do or what you usually do: カタカナがよめるようになった, "I've become able to read katakana". title: 〜ようだ・〜みたい — "seems"
explanation: Use ようだ, or casual みたい, when you draw a conclusion from what you notice: だれもいないようです, "it seems nobody's here". Put it after a plain-form sentence; nouns take のようだ or just みたい (あめのようだ, あめみたい), and な-adjectives take なようだ or just みたい (ひまみたい). みたい is what you'll hear and say most with your partner, while ようです is more careful and polite. title: 〜なくてもいい — "don't have to"
explanation: To say "you don't have to …", take the ない-form, change ない to なくて, and add もいい: いそがなくてもいい, "you don't have to hurry". title: 〜なら — "if it's …"
explanation: なら means "if (as you say)" or "if it's about …", and it usually builds on something the other person has just said: きょうとにいくなら、あきがいいよ, "if you're going to Kyoto, autumn is best". Unlike たら, the なら part doesn't have to happen first: you pick autumn before you go to Kyoto. ば and と are the other "if" words, for general conditions and automatic results.

title: Passive — "was done (to me)"
explanation: The passive form says what was done to someone: う-verbs change the last u-sound to a and add れる (ふむ → ふまれる, いう → いわれる), る-verbs add られる (たべる → たべられる), する becomes される and くる becomes こられる. The person who did it is marked with に: つまにおこられた, "I got told off by my wife". Japanese also uses the passive for things that happen to you and annoy you, even the weather: あめにふられた, "I got caught in the rain". る-verb passives look exactly like the potential form, and the same shape is also used as a polite honorific, so let the context guide you; the causative (させる, "make someone do") is a different form. You only need to recognise passives for now, in casual and polite speech alike.

title: 〜ことにする — "decide to"
explanation: Add ことにする to the dictionary form or the ない-form to say you decide to do (or not to do) something: らいげつひっこすことにした, "we've decided to move next month". You'll mostly hear it in the past, ことにしました or casual ことにした, to report a decision. ことにしている means it's your personal rule or habit: まいあさはしることにしている, "I make a point of running every morning". When a decision is made by others or by circumstances, Japanese says ことになる (ことになった, "it's been decided"); just recognise it for now. Don't confuse it with ようになる, which is a gradual change rather than a decision; にする alone picks a thing (コーヒーにする).

title: 〜ても — "even if"
explanation: Add も to the て-form to say "even if" or "even though": あめがふっても、いきます, "I'll go even if it rains"; い-adjectives become くても (さむくても), and nouns and な-adjectives use でも (あめでも, ひまでも). With a question word it means "no matter …": いくらたべても、ふとらない, "no matter how much I eat, I don't put on weight". Don't confuse it with てもいい ("it's okay to …"), which gives permission. たら says what will happen if something happens, while ても says the result stays the same anyway; のに, coming later, is for frustrating real-life contrasts. It works in casual and polite speech alike.

title: 〜ところ — "about to", "in the middle of", "just did"
explanation: ところ means "point" or "moment", and the verb form in front tells you which moment: dictionary form + ところ is "just about to" (いまでるところ, "I'm just about to leave"), ている + ところ is "right in the middle of" (たべているところ), and た + ところ is "have just done" (いまついたところ, "I've just arrived"). It's perfect for quick messages to your partner. Add です for polite speech or だ in casual speech, or drop it altogether in a text. ている on its own just says something is going on; ているところ stresses "right at this very moment".

title: Honorific and humble verbs
pattern: いらっしゃる・{召|め}し{上|あ}がる・いただく・{申|もう}す
explanation: Staff in shops, hotels and on the phone use special respectful verbs, and you'll hear them every time you travel in Japan. Honorific verbs lift up the other person: いらっしゃる (be, come, go), めしあがる (eat, drink), おっしゃる (say), なさる (do), ごらんになる (look) and くださる (give me). Humble verbs lower yourself: いただく (receive, eat), まいる (come, go), もうす (say, be called), おる (be) and いたす (do). Ordinary verbs can also become honorific with お〜になる (おまちになる) or humble with お〜する (おもちします, "let me carry that"), and passive-looking forms like こられる are sometimes used as light honorifics too. You only need to recognise these, alongside set phrases like いらっしゃいませ; when you speak, ordinary ます-forms are perfectly polite.

title: 〜か — questions inside sentences
explanation: To tuck a question inside a bigger sentence, end the question part with か: なんじにはじまるかわからない, "I don't know what time it starts". If the question has no question word (a yes/no question), use かどうか, "whether or not": くるかどうかきいてみる, "I'll ask whether she's coming". Use the plain form before か, but drop だ after nouns and な-adjectives: ほんとうかどうか, "whether it's true". The bigger verb is usually わからない, しらない, おぼえていない, きいてみる or おしえて. It works in casual and polite speech; just make the last verb polite (わかりません).

title: 〜てほしい — "I want you to"
explanation: On its own, ほしい means you want a thing (なにがほしい？); after the て-form it means you want someone else to do something: もっとはなしてほしい, "I want you to talk to me more". The person you want to act takes に: おっとにてつだってほしい, "I want my husband to help". For "I don't want you to …", use the ない-form + でほしい: しんぱいしないでほしい. Said straight to someone it can sound demanding, so for everyday requests the softer 〜てくれる？ or 〜てもらえる？ usually works better. Add です for polite speech (〜てほしいです), or soften it with な or んだけど with your partner.

title: 〜のに — "even though"
explanation: のに links two facts when the second is unexpected, disappointing or annoying: やくそくしたのに、こなかった, "even though he promised, he didn't come". Use the plain form before のに, but nouns and な-adjectives take な (やすみなのに, ひまなのに). At the end of a sentence のに shows regret or a mild complaint: いっしょにいきたかったのに, "and I really wanted to go with you". けど is a neutral "but", and ても is "even if" about things that may happen, while のに is about real facts and carries feeling. It works in casual and polite speech, but because it sounds like a complaint, use it gently with your partner!

title: Causative — "make / let someone"
explanation: The causative form says someone makes or lets another person do something. Build it from the ない-form stem: う-verbs change the last u-sound to a and add せる (いく → いかせる, まつ → またせる), る-verbs add させる (たべる → たべさせる), する becomes させる and くる becomes こさせる. The person who is made or allowed to act usually takes に: こどもにやさいをたべさせる, "I make the kids eat vegetables". The set phrase 〜させてください means "please let me …" (はらわせてください, "let me pay"), and おまたせしました, "sorry to keep you waiting", comes from the same form. Don't mix it up with the passive (〜れる・〜られる, "was done to me"); you only need to recognise causatives for now.
